analysis.one_liner: Creates a public federal database of corporate crimes and enforcement actions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Bureau of Justice Statistics to collect every federal enforcement action against a corporation — criminal cases, civil suits, settlements, deferred-prosecution and non-prosecution agreements — and publish them in a free, searchable online database. Each entry would name the company, its parent company, the agency involved, the violation, and the outcome, and the Bureau would report yearly to Congress on corporate crime patterns and enforcement gaps. The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, workers, investors, and journalists who want to see which companies have been cited or charged for federal violations — from wage theft to fraud to pollution — without paying for commercial legal databases. Because the database would link subsidiaries to parent companies, it would also expose repeat offenders hiding behind corporate structures, and the annual report would give Congress and regulators data on how often companies reoffend.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Bureau of Justice Statistics to build a public, searchable, downloadable database of every federal enforcement action against corporations and their employees, including deferred and non-prosecution agreements.
Would name the specific companies and their parent companies in each enforcement action, so consumers and workers could see a firm's full record even when violations happen at a subsidiary.
Requires an annual report to Congress analyzing corporate crime recidivism and its impact on victims, with recommendations for improving federal enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies and their parent corporations, whose violations, settlements, and non-prosecution agreements would become far easier for the public to find in one place. Federal agencies would also bear the administrative cost of regularly submitting enforcement records to the Bureau of Justice Statistics.

drawbacks.text: The database requires federal agencies to compile and submit enforcement records, an administrative burden with no new funding specified in the bill text, which could slow agency work or produce uneven data quality across agencies.

Publishing 'alleged' violations, including cases that ended in declinations or settlements with no admission of wrongdoing, could publicize unproven allegations against companies and individuals before any adjudication.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: better public visibility into corporate lawbreaking could help consumers, workers, journalists, and regulators spot repeat offenders, and the annual report would give Congress data on enforcement gaps. The costs are small — mainly agency time to compile and standardize records — but the bill's benefit depends entirely on agencies reporting accurately, and it creates no new enforcement power or penalty; it only makes existing enforcement records easier to see.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Oversight committees in December 2023 and neither committee acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2023 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Oversight and Accountability Committee.
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025.
It attracted 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, which limited any pressure to move it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies facing federal enforcement keep enforcement records scattered across agency websites; the public gains nothing.

industries.industry: Corporations under federal enforcement (banks, drug makers, polluters, defense contractors, etc.)
industries.note: The bill would compile every federal enforcement action, settlement, and non-prosecution agreement against them into one public, searchable database with parent-company links, making repeat-offender patterns visible to consumers, workers, journalists, and courts.
Agencies would face new data-collection and reporting duties, but the public visibility could strengthen their enforcement leverage; the bill assigns the work without new funding.
